title: Functions I
subtitle: First Recipes
martuIntro:
At the Institute we called these recipes. You write the steps once and give them a name. When you need them, you call the name.
Some recipes need ingredients. Some hand something back.
You have met recipes already: `def move_left():` at the cabin door, `perform_roll(die_size)` at the trap door. Recipes were the hardest wall in the campaign, for everyone. Today we take that wall apart, one stone at a time, yes?
goals: Tell `=` (a box) from `def` (a recipe), and know that making a recipe does not run it
Call a recipe with `()`, and replace `pass` with a real step, indented under the `def` line
Give a recipe ingredients (parameters), and use their names inside it so every call works
Hand a value back with `return`, catch it in a box, and know why a recipe with no `return` gives `None`
Trace a call: what goes in, what each box holds, and what comes back
Store what one recipe hands back, then pass it on to another, like the dialogue prompt in Module 1
Hand back a comparison with `return roll >= needed`, and roll with `random.randint(1, die_size)`

items.title: Mar'tu remembers…
items.summary: Two quick questions from earlier lessons. Nothing is scored.

whyWrong.0: `=` puts 20 in the box. Read it as gets: roll gets 20. It asks nothing.

questions.explain: `==` asks: is the same as? `roll == 20` gives `True` or `False`. `=` puts a value in a box.
Python works out the right side first: 26 - 3 is 23. Then `mana` gets 23. The box now holds the new value.

items.title: Recipes With Names
items.summary: Make recipes with `def`, call them, give them ingredients, hand values back with `return`, and rebuild the campaign's movement, dialogue and skill-check recipes.

exercises.title: A box or a recipe?
exercises.martu:
A [[variable|box]] holds a value. A [[recipe]] holds steps.
`=` makes a box. [[def]] makes a recipe: `def`, a name, `()` and a colon. The steps go under it, indented.
Making a recipe does not run it. Python reads it and remembers it. To run it, you [[call]] it: its name, then `()`.
You have seen this at the cabin door, yes? `def move_left():` waited for the arrow key. Now you know why.

anotherWay.label: Box and card side by side
anotherWay.text:
```text
box:    name = value
        holds one value

recipe: def name():
            step
        holds steps

call:   name()
        runs the steps
```

anotherWay.label: A jar and a recipe card
anotherWay.text: A jar holds one thing: sugar. A recipe card holds steps: mix, stir, bake. Writing the card bakes nothing. You bake when you follow the card. `say_steady()` is following the card.

anotherWay.label: What Python does
anotherWay.text:
1. `steadying_words = ...`: Python makes the box.
2. `def say_steady():`: Python reads the recipe and remembers it. It runs nothing.
3. The end of the file. Nothing called the recipe, so nothing printed.
4. Add `say_steady()`: now Python runs the recipe's step, and `Steady, now.` prints.

anotherWay.label: Not this
anotherWay.text: Not this: `def ("mana")`. `def` never makes a box. A box is `mana = 20`. A recipe is `def say_steady():` with its steps indented under it.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: At the cabin door, `def move_left():` made a recipe. The game called `move_left()` when you pressed the left arrow. No arrow, no call, no step. Same here: no `say_steady()`, no words.
My recipes sit in a book on the mantle. They do nothing there. Only when someone reads one out loud does anything happen.

checkpoints.text: Call the recipe: add `say_steady()` at the bottom.
hints: Nothing calls the recipe yet, so its step never runs. Where does a recipe get called? Below its `def` block, on a line of its own.
A name with `()` after it runs that recipe. If `def hum():` makes a recipe, then `hum()` on its own line runs it.
Write `say_steady()` on a new line at the bottom, with no spaces in front.

campaignLink.why: You have seen this at the cabin door. Each `def` line made a recipe. The game called `move_left()` when you pressed the left arrow. Making the recipe never moved the party: only the call did.

exercises.takeaway: `=` makes a box. `def` makes a recipe. Making it runs nothing; `name()` calls it.

predict.q: Before you press Run: what will this print?
predict.explain:
Only `Oogrish waits.` The `def` block makes the recipe, and Python remembers it. Nothing inside runs, because no line calls `say_steady()`.
Run the starter: it prints nothing at all, for the same reason.

exercises.title: Call it
exercises.martu:
The lines [[indent|indented]] under `def` are the recipe's steps. They belong to it. They run only when the recipe is called, and they run together, top to bottom.
Give Gearshift's report a second line. Then call it.
A recipe needs at least one step inside. An empty one makes Python stop.

anotherWay.label: The indent means: belongs to the recipe
anotherWay.text:
1. `def barrier_report():` starts the recipe.
2. Every line under it with four spaces in front is a step of that recipe.
3. The first line with no spaces ends the recipe.
4. `barrier_report()` with no spaces runs all the steps, top to bottom.

anotherWay.label: Inside and outside
anotherWay.text:
```text
def barrier_report():
    step 1   <- inside
    step 2   <- inside

barrier_report()  <- outside:
                     the call
```
Steps: indented under `def`. The call: no spaces, with `()`.

```python
def tidy():

tidy()
```

exercises.title: Ingredients
exercises.martu:
Some recipes need an ingredient. Its name goes in the brackets on the `def` line: a [[parameter]].
When you call the recipe, you hand over a real value: an [[argument]]. For that one call, Python puts it in the parameter, like a box.
The Example hands over two names, one per call. Same recipe, a different hero each time.
My check also calls `warn` with heroes you never wrote, like `warn("Tester")`. One line inside must work for every hero.

anotherWay.label: The call table
anotherWay.text:
```text
call                hero_name
warn("Lucky")       "Lucky"
warn("Bomb Shell")  "Bomb Shell"
```
One recipe. Each call fills `hero_name` with something new.

anotherWay.label: A fill-in card
anotherWay.text: A fill-in card says: "____, get inside!" Each time you read it out, you put a different name in the blank. `hero_name` is that blank, with a name of its own.

anotherWay.label: It is a box
anotherWay.text: `hero_name` is a box, like the boxes from Unit 1. The call fills it. `warn("Lucky")` works like `hero_name = "Lucky"`, just before the recipe's steps run.

1. `warn("Lucky")`: `hero_name` gets `"Lucky"`.
2. The step runs: `hero_name + ", get inside!"` is `Lucky, get inside!`
3. `warn("Bomb Shell")`: `hero_name` gets `"Bomb Shell"`, and the same step runs again.
When the clock nears the arc, I shout the same warning at each of you. Only the name changes. That is a recipe with one ingredient.

exercises.title: Use the ingredients
exercises.martu:
Inside the recipe, use the ingredient names, never the numbers from one call. The numbers arrive when the recipe is called.
Remember the chalk math in Unit 1? Show your working with boxes, not the answer. Same here: `base_damage` and `bonus` are the boxes.
Two calls are written for you. One line inside the recipe must work for both.

anotherWay.label: The call table
anotherWay.text:
```text
call            base_damage bonus
show_hit(4, 3)  4           3
show_hit(8, 2)  8           2
```
`base_damage + bonus` is 7 in the first row and 10 in the second. `4 + 3` would be 7 in both.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? The recipe can't know the numbers yet
anotherWay.text: When Python reads the `def` line, nobody has called the recipe. There are no numbers yet. `show_hit(4, 3)` brings 4 and 3. `show_hit(8, 2)` brings 8 and 2. Type `4 + 3` inside, and the second call still shows 7.

anotherWay.label: A fill-in card
anotherWay.text: The card says: add ____ and ____. You fill the blanks each time you read it. Write 4 and 3 on the card in ink, and every reading says 7.

anotherWay.label: Ingredients arrive at the call
anotherWay.text:
```text
show_hit(8, 2)
         |  |
         v  v
  base_damage=8
  bonus=2
  print(8 + 2) -> 10
```

exercises.title: Send it back
exercises.martu:
`print` says the answer out loud to the room. [[return]] writes it on a note and hands it back to the line that called.
Catch the note in a box: `lucky_max = max_mana_for(13)`. If nothing catches it, it is gone.
A recipe with no `return` hands back [[None]], Python's word for nothing.
Try it after step 2: delete `return total`, run, and see what `lucky_max` holds. Then put it back. Your ticks come back when you do.

anotherWay.label: The return arrow
anotherWay.text:
```text
lucky_max = max_mana_for(13)
    ^             |
    |    affinity = 13
    |    total = 26
    +--- return total
```
The note comes back to the call, and the box on the left catches it.

anotherWay.label: A note handed back
anotherWay.text: You ask a friend to add up the bill. `print` is them shouting the total across the room. `return` is them writing it on a note and handing it to you. You can keep a note.

anotherWay.label: Step table
anotherWay.text:
1. `max_mana_for(13)`: `affinity` gets 13.
2. `total = affinity * 2`: `total` gets 26.
3. `return total`: the recipe hands back 26 and ends.
4. `lucky_max = ...`: the box catches 26.
5. `print(lucky_max)` shows 26.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? `return` ends the recipe
anotherWay.text:
`return` hands the note back, and the recipe stops there. A line under it, inside the recipe, never runs:
```python
def double(n):
    return n * 2
    print("Never shown.")
```
`double(4)` hands back 8 and prints nothing.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: At the trap door, `perform_roll(die_size)` handed back a roll with `return`. The skill check caught it and compared it. A recipe that hands back is a recipe you can use again.
At the Institute, apprentices wrote answers on slips and passed them up. A shouted answer helped nobody at the back. A slip could be kept.

exercises.title: Be the ledger
exercises.martu:
Be the ledger, yes? Read this spell. You run it in your head, not on the screen.
```python
def ward_strength(lanterns, runes):
    light = lanterns * 10
    glow = runes * 5
    return light + glow

barrier = ward_strength(3, 4) + 10
print(barrier)
```
Fill one row at a time: what each box holds when it runs. Use what is IN the boxes, not the numbers written in the recipe.
Fill every row before you look anything up.

anotherWay.label: The return arrow, with another call
anotherWay.text:
Here is the same recipe with another call. Do yours the same way.
```text
ward_strength(4, 3) + 10
  lanterns = 4
  runes = 3
  light = 40
  glow = 15
  return 55 ----+
                |
barrier = 55 + 10
        = 65
```

anotherWay.label: Step by step, with another call
anotherWay.text:
Here is the same recipe with another call. Do yours the same way.
1. `ward_strength(4, 3)` hands over 4 and 3: `lanterns` is 4, `runes` is 3.
2. `light` is 4 times 10: 40.
3. `glow` is 3 times 5: 15.
4. The recipe hands back 40 + 15: 55.
5. `barrier` is 55 + 10: 65.
6. `print(barrier)` shows 65, and only 65.

solution: # The ledger: what each box holds
exercises.takeaway: Trace a call with what is IN the boxes. What the recipe hands back lands where the call was.
exercises.pairTalk: Pair talk: fill your ledger on your own first. Then compare rows with your partner. Where do you differ? Find the line in the program that settles it.

exercises.title: Return the right box
exercises.martu: Two recipes, two slips: one crashes, one is quiet. Read Python's last line first, then mend them one at a time.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? Whose kitchen is `result` in?
anotherWay.text: `result` was made inside `triple`, in my Example. A box made inside a recipe lives in that recipe's kitchen only. `armor_total` has its own kitchen, and its box is `total`.

anotherWay.label: Two kitchens
anotherWay.text:
```text
triple's kitchen:
  result

armor_total's kitchen:
  total   <- hand this back
```

anotherWay.label: The wrong bowl
anotherWay.text: You cook soup in the blue bowl, then hand over the red bowl from yesterday's kitchen. It isn't here. Hand over the bowl you just filled.

1. Read the message: `name 'result' is not defined`.
2. Find the box the recipe makes: `total = base + bonus`.
3. Hand that one back: `return total`.
4. Run. `Shield: None` means the second recipe has no `return`. Add one.
Hand back the box you made. No `return` means `None`.

exercises.title: Store, then pass it on
exercises.martu:
`get_greeting()` hands back a line. Look how it tidies the line: `.lower()` makes every letter small, then [[.capitalize()]] makes the first letter big.
`present_greeting()` must store that line in a variable (a box), then pass the variable on to the Ley board.
Three moves: call the helper, store what it hands back, pass it on. You did this in Module 1, yes? Now you see why it works.

anotherWay.text: Module 1: `get_dialogue_prompt_string()` handed back Mar'tu's line. `present_dialogue_option()` stored it in a variable, then passed that variable to `print_prompt()`. Same three moves.

anotherWay.label: Three moves
anotherWay.text:
1. Call the helper: `get_greeting()`.
2. Store what it hands back: `greeting = get_greeting()`.
3. Pass it on: `show_on_ley_board(greeting)`.

exercises.martu:
A skill check hands back `True` or `False`. The Example shows two ways to write one: an `if` that returns `True` or `False`, and one short line.
`roll >= needed` is already a question with a True or False answer. So you can hand back the answer itself: `return roll >= needed`.

anotherWay.text:
1. `roll >= needed` is a question. Python answers it: `True` or `False`.
2. The long form asks it in an `if`, then hands back `True` or `False` by hand.
3. The short form hands back the answer straight away. Same result, one line.

```text
1 ... needed-1 | needed ... 20
     False     |     True
```

exercises.title: A rolling recipe
exercises.martu:
At the trap door, `perform_roll(die_size)` rolled the dice for every check. Now you write that recipe yourself.
`die_size` is the ingredient: how many faces the die has. 6 for a d6, 20 for a d20.
`random.randint(1, 6)` rolls a d6, both ends included. Here, the number of faces arrives in the ingredient.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: Module 2, the trap door: `perform_roll(die_size)` handed back `random.randint(1, die_size)`. Every check called it. One recipe, any die.

1. `roll_die(6)`: `die_size` gets 6.
2. `random.randint(1, die_size)` rolls from 1 to 6.
3. `return` hands that roll back to the line that called.

anotherWay.label: A die with die_size faces
anotherWay.text:
```text
roll_die(6)   ->  1 to 6
roll_die(20)  ->  1 to 20
die_size sets the top face.
```

items.title: Recipe Quiz
items.summary: Eight questions on making, calling and tracing recipes. Retake as often as you like.

questions.explain: `4 * 5` is written in ink, so every call shows 20. `cells * 5` would show 35 for this call.
The call prints 26 while it runs. But the recipe has no `return`, so it hands back `None`, and `lucky_max` holds `None`. `print` shows; `return` hands back.

questions.q: Trace it like the ledger. What will this print?
questions.explain:
`lanterns` holds 2 and `runes` holds 8. `light` is 20, `glow` is 40, so the recipe hands back 60. Then 60 + 10 is 70.
60 forgets the `+ 10` on the `barrier` line. 50 starts from `glow` (40 + 10), not from what the recipe hands back. 25 adds the numbers written in the recipe (10 + 5 + 10). 20 adds the numbers handed over (2 + 8 + 10).
`>=` means at least. 10 is one short: `False`. 11 is exactly enough: `True`. 12 is more: `True`. The recipe hands back the answer, not the roll.

questions.q: In `warn("Lucky")`, which part is the argument (what you hand over)?

whyWrong.0: `warn` is the recipe's name. It says which recipe to run.
whyWrong.2: `hero_name` is the parameter: the ingredient's name on the card. It holds the argument during the call.
whyWrong.3: The brackets make the call happen. What goes inside them is the argument.

questions.explain: The argument is the value you hand over: `"Lucky"`. During the call, the parameter `hero_name` holds it.

questions.q: Put the lines in order (with their indents) so the program shows Mar'tu's greeting. Store it in a variable first, then pass it on.
questions.explain: Call the helper, store what it hands back in `greeting`, then pass `greeting` on. With no `()`, `get_greeting` is the recipe itself, not its line.

whyWrong.1: The recipe works out 14 in `left`, but it hands back `result`, a box this recipe never made.
whyWrong.2: `None` comes from a recipe with no `return` line. This one has a `return`, and it names a box that doesn't exist, so Python stops.

questions.explain: `mana_after`'s box is `left`. `return result` stops Python: name 'result' is not defined. Write `return left`.
`double(4)` hands back 8, and `y` catches it. Then `y + 1` is 9.

This recipe [[hands back]] its answer. `price` is the ingredient: the price of one thing. The recipe hands back twice that, with `return`.

anotherWay.label: The note handed back
anotherWay.text:
```text
print(double_cost(4))
      price = 4
      4 * 2 = 8
      return 8 --+
                 |
print(   8   ) <-+
```
`print` says the answer out loud to the room. `return` writes it on a note and hands it to whoever called. Here the caller is `print(...)`, which shows the note.
1. `double_cost(4)` puts 4 in `price`. 2. `price * 2` is 8. 3. `return` hands 8 back to the call. 4. `print` shows 8. The next call puts 15 in `price`.

items.martu:
Lucky worked out his supply run by hand. It works, yes? But if the prices change, three lines and a typed total all need mending by hand. A recipe does the work once.
Write `item_cost`, let each cost line call it, and let `total_cost` add the boxes. Mar'tu's check swaps in other prices, only inside the check, so your boxes must follow.

anotherWay.label: A price list
anotherWay.text: Sums scribbled on a receipt go stale when a price changes. A price list on the wall does not: change it once, and every line that reads it follows. `item_cost` is the price list.

1. Write `item_cost(count, price)` at the top. It hands back the count times the price. 2. Swap each old sum for a call with the same two numbers. 3. Make `total_cost` add the three boxes. 4. Keep the print.

exercises.title: Trace the call
exercises.martu:
Trace it like the ledger: what does the call hand back, and what does the last line print?
```python
def ward_strength(lanterns, runes):
    light = lanterns * 10
    glow = runes * 5
    return light + glow

barrier = ward_strength(2, 5) + 10
print(barrier)
```
Stuck? Skip it, or try the lesson Recipes With Names. Tasks you pass here stay ticked.

anotherWay.label: Another call
anotherWay.text:
```text
ward_strength(5, 4)
  lanterns = 5
  runes = 4
  light = 50
  glow = 20
  return 70 ----+
                |
barrier = 70 + 10
```

Your own skill check, in a recipe. Pick how hard it is. Then hand back `True` when the roll is high enough, and `False` when it is not. Exactly enough counts. Mar'tu's check tries every kind of roll.

items.title: Quick Check Recipes I · Form A questions
items.summary: Four questions that go with Quick Check Recipes I. To pass the Quick Check, get 3 of the 4 right.

whyWrong.0: `def` never makes a box. Python stops at once: it expects `(` after the name.
whyWrong.2: `def` makes a recipe, not a box. It needs indented steps under it, and holds no value.

questions.explain: A box is a name, `=`, and a value: `hero = "Lucky"`. `def` makes a recipe.
The recipe works out 17 and keeps it in `shield`, but it has no `return`. So the call hands back `None`, and `lucky_shield` holds `None`.
Numbers typed inside the recipe are written in ink: every call shows 15, whatever it hands over. To use the 2 and the 9, the recipe needs its ingredients, `count * price`.
`.lower()` makes every letter small. Then `.capitalize()` makes only the first letter big.

exercises.title: Trace the call
exercises.martu:
Trace it like the ledger: what does the call hand back, and what does the last line print?
```python
def glow_total(candles, runes):
    light = candles * 4
    shine = runes * 3
    return light + shine

room = glow_total(5, 3) + 10
print(room)
```
Stuck? Skip it, or try the lesson Recipes With Names. Tasks you pass here stay ticked.

anotherWay.label: Another call
anotherWay.text:
```text
glow_total(3, 5)
  candles = 3
  runes = 5
  light = 12
  shine = 15
  return 27 ----+
                |
room = 27 + 10
```
1. The call fills `candles` and `runes`, in order. 2. Work out `light` and `shine` from what is IN them. 3. `return` hands back `light + shine`. 4. The last line adds 10, and `print` shows `room`.

exercises.martu:
Your own skill check, in a recipe. Pick how hard it is. Then hand back `True` when the roll is high enough, and `False` when it is not. Exactly enough counts. Mar'tu's check tries every kind of roll.
Stuck? Skip it, or try the lesson Recipes With Names. Tasks you pass here stay ticked.

```text
1 ... needed-1 | needed ... 20
     False     |    True
```

items.title: Quick Check Recipes I · Form B questions
items.summary: Four questions that go with Quick Check Recipes I. To pass the Quick Check, get 3 of the 4 right.

whyWrong.0: `def` never makes a box. Python stops at once: it expects `(` after the name.
whyWrong.2: `def` makes a recipe, not a box. It needs indented steps under it, and holds no value.

questions.explain: A box is a name, `=`, and a value: `spell = "Fireball"`. `def` makes a recipe.
The recipe works out 15 and keeps it in `fuel`, but it has no `return`. So the call hands back `None`, and `tank` holds `None`.
Numbers typed inside the recipe are written in ink: every call shows 8, whatever it hands over. To use the 4 and the 5, the recipe needs its ingredients, `base + bonus`.
`.lower()` makes every letter small. Then `.capitalize()` makes only the first letter big.

items.title: Mar'tu's Chalk Notes: Recipes
items.summary: Everything from Unit 3 on one page. Printable.

entries.note: `def` makes a recipe (a function): a named set of steps, indented under it. Making it runs nothing. Its name with `()` calls it. (Lesson: Recipes With Names)

entries.concept: `=` makes a box, `def` makes a recipe
entries.note: A box holds a value. A recipe holds steps. `def` never makes a box.
`pass` means do nothing. Replace it with real steps, indented. You've seen this: `move_left()` with `party.move("left")`.

entries.concept: Ingredients and what you hand over
entries.output:
Lucky, get inside!
Bomb Shell, get inside!
entries.note: `hero_name` is the ingredient (parameter) on the card. `"Lucky"` is what you hand over (argument). Each call fills the ingredient fresh.

entries.concept: Use the ingredients, never one call's numbers
entries.note: `print(4 + 3)` inside would show 7 for every call. The numbers arrive when the recipe is called.
`return` hands the answer back to the call. `lucky_max = ...` catches it in a box.
`print` only shows the answer. With no `return`, the call hands back `None`.
Hand back the box this recipe made, `total`. A name from an example, like `result`, is not here.
Write each box's value: lamps 4, nights 2, oil 8, spare 6. The call hands back 14, so `stock` is 15. Use what is IN the boxes. (Lesson: Recipes With Names, Be the ledger)
Call the helper, store what it hands back in a variable, then pass that variable on. You've seen this: `present_dialogue_option()`.
`.lower()` makes every letter small. `.capitalize()` makes only the first letter big.
`roll >= needed` is already `True` or `False`, so hand it back. An `if` with `return True` and `else:` `return False` does the same. You've seen this: `return roll >= required_roll`.
The ingredient decides the faces: `roll_die(6)` is a d6. You've seen this: `perform_roll(die_size)`.
